title: Quiz: genomic intervals
text:
Short questions on coordinates, file formats and interval operations. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A BED file contains the line chr3  499  500. Which base is this, as a 1-based position? How long is the interval?






Hint





BED counts the boundaries between bases from 0.









Answer





Base 500 (1-based), chr3:500-500. Length \(500 - 499 = 1\): a single base.




Q2. You copy SNP positions from a VCF into a BED file as chrom  pos  pos+1. What is wrong, and what happens when you intersect the file with a list of CpG sites?






Hint





VCF is 1-based. What is the BED start of the base at 1-based position pos?









Answer





The base at 1-based position pos is pos−1  pos in BED. Writing pos  pos+1 shifts every SNP one base to the right, so SNPs on the C of a CpG appear on the G, and SNPs on the G appear outside the CpG. Some true overlaps are missed and some false ones are reported.




Q3. A narrowPeak line ends in … 12.4  35.1  32.8  210, and its start is 1 000 000. Where is the summit, and what is its \(q\)-value?






Hint





The last column is an offset from the start; the \(p\) and \(q\) columns are \(-\log_{10}\).









Answer





Summit boundary \(1\,000\,000 + 210 = 1\,000\,210\) (BED 1000210  1000211, 1-based position 1 000 211). \(q = 10^{-32.8}\).




Q4. A gene is on the − strand, from 50 000 to 60 000 (1-based). Where is its TSS, and in which direction is “upstream”?






Answer





The TSS is at 60 000, the end coordinate. Upstream is towards larger coordinates (60 001, 60 002, …).




Q5. bedtools intersect -a peaks.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l gives 12 000 and the peak file has 10 000 lines. Your colleague concludes that more than 100% of the peaks are at promoters. What went wrong, and what command should they run?






Answer





The default output has one line per overlapping (peak, promoter) pair, and a peak overlapping several promoter windows (alternative TSSs) is counted several times. Count peaks with bedtools intersect -u -a peaks.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l, then divide by 10 000.




Q6. A = chr1 100 200, B = chr1 150 400, C = chr1 400 500. What does cat A B C | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge return?






Hint





Do B and C overlap, or only touch? By default merge also joins intervals that touch (book-ended).









Answer





A and B overlap, so they merge into 100–400. B ends at boundary 400 and C starts there: they touch without sharing a base, and bedtools merge joins book-ended intervals by default. The result is one interval, chr1 100 500.




Q7. Your peaks overlap enhancers 4 times more often than shuffled peaks do. The shuffle placed peaks anywhere in the genome file, including centromeres and runs of N. Is the true enrichment likely higher or lower than 4?






Answer





Lower. Shuffled peaks in impossible places (gaps, centromeres, unmappable repeats) never overlap anything, so the shuffled overlap is too low and the enrichment too high. Restrict the shuffle (-chrom, -excl blacklist and gaps, or -incl the mappable genome) for a fairer null.




Q8. You read a BED file with read.table() and build GRanges(V1, IRanges(V2, V3)). What is wrong with the result, and how do you avoid it?






Answer





Every range is one base too long on the left: the 0-based BED start is used as a 1-based start. Use rtracklayer::import(), which converts, or add 1 to the start (IRanges(V2 + 1, V3)), or makeGRangesFromDataFrame(..., starts.in.df.are.0based = TRUE).




Q9. Peak files from two labs give a Jaccard index of 0.02. Can you conclude that the two peak sets are unrelated?






Answer





No. Jaccard counts shared bases relative to the union. If one set has narrow peaks (a TF) and the other broad ones (a histone mark), even complete overlap of every narrow peak gives a small Jaccard. Count overlapping peaks and compare with a shuffled null instead.




Q10. One file has chr1, the other 1; one is hg19, the other hg38. Which of the two problems will bedtools tell you about?






Answer





Neither reliably. With different chromosome names nothing overlaps, so you get an empty or suspiciously small result (sometimes a warning). With different builds the names match, so bedtools reports overlaps, just wrong ones, with no error. Always check build and naming before you start.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Background
Coordinates. BED and bedGraph count the boundaries between bases from 0, so an interval start end covers the bases after boundary start up to boundary end: length = end − start. GTF, SAM, VCF and GRanges number the bases from 1 and include both ends: length = end − start + 1. To go from 1-based [s, e] to BED: s − 1, e.
narrowPeak is BED6 + 4 columns: signalValue (enrichment), pValue and qValue (both as \(-\log_{10}\), −1 = not available), and peak, the summit as an offset from start.
Strand. The TSS of a transcript is its start on the + strand and its end on the − strand. Upstream of a − strand gene is towards higher coordinates.
Overlap counts and chance. Overlap by default means at least one shared base. Report each peak once (-u) when counting peaks. Whether an overlap is more than chance needs a null: shuffle one set to random positions (same widths) many times and compare.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Data
The exercise uses three GM12878 peak sets from ENCODE (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, CTCF; GRCh38), the GENCODE v46 basic annotation, the hg38 chromosome sizes, and the ENCODE blacklist. From the course repository:
data/download.sh genomic-intervals      # about 35 MB
mkdir -p ~/epi/intervals && cd ~/epi/intervals
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
You need bedtools and the usual Unix tools (see Install the software you need). Everything runs in seconds on a laptop or a login node; on the cluster you can also wrap the commands in an sbatch script.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Coordinates.

A VCF file reports a SNP at chr7  117559590 (1-based). Write the BED line for this single base.
A BED line reads chr2  1000  1250. Write the region as a browser would display it (1-based), and give its length.
A GTF exon is chr1  11869  12227  +. Write it as a BED line and give its length.
Two BED intervals chr1 100 200 and chr1 200 300. Do they overlap? Do they share a base?

B2. A narrowPeak line. This is the first line of the ENCODE CTCF file:
chr12  53676107  53676353  .  1000  .  497.29450  -1.00000  4.87269  126

How wide is the peak?
At which position is the summit? Give it as a one-base BED interval and as a 1-based position.
What does −1 in column 8 mean? What \(q\)-value does column 9 correspond to?
Can you use column 5 to rank peaks by strength? Which column would you use?

B3. Promoters and strand. A transcript is annotated in a GTF as chr5  1000000  1050000 on the − strand.

Where is its TSS (1-based)?
Define the promoter as 2 kb upstream to 500 bp downstream of the TSS. Give it as a 1-based interval and as a BED line.
A script computes every promoter as start − 2000 to start + 500, ignoring strand. Where does this put the window for this transcript, and what lies there?

B4. Interval operations. On a 1000 bp genome (chrT, BED coordinates):
A:  chrT 100 300    chrT 500 600    chrT 700 900
B:  chrT 250 450    chrT 850 950
Draw A and B on a ruler, then give the output of:

bedtools intersect -a A -b B (b) intersect -u (c) intersect -v (d) subtract -a A -b B
cat A B | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge (f) closest -a A -b B -d (the distance column) (g) complement -i A with the genome file chrT 1000.

B5. Counting overlaps. bedtools intersect -u -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l gives 21 390, but the same command without -u gives 63 214 lines. The H3K4me3 file has 53 912 peaks.

What fraction of the H3K4me3 peaks overlap a promoter?
How can the default output have more lines than there are peaks? Think about what a gene with many transcripts looks like in the promoter file.

B6. Overlaps by hand in R terms. Queries q1 = [1, 10], q2 = [20, 40], q3 = [50, 60]; subjects s1 = [5, 25], s2 = [35, 55] (1-based, as in GRanges). Write the result of findOverlaps(q, s) as a table of (query, subject) pairs, and give countOverlaps(q, s) and overlapsAny(q, s).
B7. Is it more than chance?

30 of your peaks overlap a set of enhancers. In 999 shuffles of the peaks, the mean overlap was 12, and 4 shuffles reached 30 or more. Compute the enrichment and the empirical \(p\)-value \((k + 1) / (N + 1)\).
In another test none of 99 shuffles reached the observed value. What is the smallest \(p\)-value you can report, and how could you report the result honestly?
A colleague shuffles peaks over the whole genome file, including chrY, unplaced contigs and the centromeres. Will the enrichment be too high or too low? Why?

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the data
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf; do
  zcat $D/gm12878_${m}_peaks.bed.gz | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > $m.bed
done
head -3 ctcf.bed
wc -l *.bed
awk '{ w = $3 - $2; s += w } END { print s / NR }' ctcf.bed      # mean width
cut -f1 ctcf.bed | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1n | head             # peaks per chromosome

How many peaks are in each file, and what is the mean width of each kind? Why are CTCF peaks so much narrower than H3K27ac peaks?
Which chromosomes appear? Is there a chrY in the CTCF file? Count the H3K27ac peaks on chrY. GM12878 comes from a woman: how do you explain what you find?



C2 — A TSS file from the GTF
zcat $D/gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz \
 | awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$3 == "transcript" && $9 ~ /transcript_type "protein_coding"/ {
     match($9, /gene_name "[^"]+"/); g = substr($9, RSTART + 11, RLENGTH - 12)
     tss = ($7 == "+") ? $4 : $5
     print $1, tss - 1, tss, g, ".", $7 }' \
 | sort -u | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > tss.bed
wc -l tss.bed
grep -w APP tss.bed

Explain each part of the awk program. Why tss - 1, tss?
APP (amyloid precursor protein, chr21) is on the − strand. Check that its TSSs are at the end of the gene: compare with the gene line, zcat $D/gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3=="gene" && $9 ~ /gene_name "APP";/' | cut -f1,4,5,7. How many distinct TSSs does APP have?
Replace sort -u | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n by sort -k1,1 -k2,2n -u. How many lines do you get now? Why fewer? (Read man sort on -u with -k.)



C3 — Promoters and the fraction of peaks at promoters
bedtools slop -i tss.bed -g $D/hg38.chrom.sizes -b 1000 > promoters.bed
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf; do
  echo $m $(bedtools intersect -u -a $m.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l) $(wc -l < $m.bed)
done

What fraction of each kind of peak overlaps a promoter (±1 kb of a protein-coding TSS)? Does the order match the table of marks in What is epigenetics?
Run the same without -u for H3K4me3 (B5).



C4 — Strong peaks and weak peaks
Only about 40% of H3K4me3 peaks are at a protein-coding promoter, although H3K4me3 is “the promoter mark”. Rank the peaks by signalValue (column 7):
sort -k7,7gr h3k4me3.bed | head -10000 | bedtools intersect -u -a - -b promoters.bed | wc -l
sort -k7,7g  h3k4me3.bed | head -10000 | bedtools intersect -u -a - -b promoters.bed | wc -l

What fraction of the 10 000 strongest and of the 10 000 weakest peaks are at a promoter?
Give two reasons why a real H3K4me3 peak could be far from a protein-coding TSS. (Hint: what else has a promoter? What does the weak end of a peak list contain?)



C5 — Candidate enhancers and distances to TSSs
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k27ac.bed -b h3k4me3.bed \
  | bedtools intersect -v -a - -b promoters.bed > enhancers.bed
wc -l enhancers.bed
for m in h3k4me3 h3k27ac ctcf enhancers; do
  bedtools closest -a $m.bed -b tss.bed -d -t first | awk '{ print $NF }' | sort -n \
    | awk -v m=$m '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print m, "median distance", a[int(NR / 2)] }'
done

How many candidate enhancers are there, and what is their median distance to the nearest protein-coding TSS? Compare with the medians for the three peak sets.
Which gene is nearest to the enhancer that is farthest from any TSS, and how far away is it? (sort -k17,17nr | head -1 on the closest output.) Is “nearest gene” a convincing target at that distance?



C6 — Merge and Jaccard
cat h3k4me3.bed h3k27ac.bed | cut -f1-3 | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge > active.bed
wc -l active.bed
bedtools jaccard -a h3k4me3.bed -b h3k27ac.bed
bedtools jaccard -a ctcf.bed    -b h3k27ac.bed

How many merged “active” regions are there? Why fewer than the sum of the two files?
The Jaccard index is (bases in the intersection) / (bases in the union). Compare the two values. Does a small Jaccard index mean that CTCF and H3K27ac are unrelated? (Hold on to your answer for C7.)



C7 — Is the CTCF–H3K27ac overlap more than chance?
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X|Y)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > genome.txt   # main chromosomes only

bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b h3k27ac.bed | wc -l        # observed

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  bedtools shuffle -i h3k27ac.bed -g genome.txt -chrom -excl blacklist.bed -seed $i \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b - | wc -l
done > shuffled.txt

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  bedtools shuffle -i h3k27ac.bed -g $D/hg38.chrom.sizes -seed $i \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools intersect -u -a ctcf.bed -b - | wc -l
done > shuffled_naive.txt

What is the observed number of CTCF peaks that overlap an H3K27ac peak? What is the mean over the 100 restricted shuffles, the enrichment, and the empirical \(p\)-value?
Compute the same enrichment with the naive shuffle. Which is larger, and why (B7c)?
Combine with C6: the overlap is highly significant, but what fraction of CTCF peaks overlap H3K27ac? Write one sentence for a results section that reports both.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
In R
You need GenomicRanges and rtracklayer (see Install the software you need). Set D to the data folder:
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Import peaks and check the coordinates
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
ctcf
raw <- read.table(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), nrows = 1)
raw$V2; start(ctcf)[1]                   # start in the file vs in R
raw$V3 - raw$V2; width(ctcf)[1]          # widths
summit <- start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak        # careful: which convention?
summit[1]

By how much do the starts differ, and do the widths agree?
Is start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak the 1-based position of the summit? Compare with your answer to B2b.
Build a GRanges yourself with GRanges(raw$V1, IRanges(raw$V2, raw$V3)). What is its width, and what went wrong? Fix it.



R2 — TSSs and promoters in R
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding"]
tss <- resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start")        # fix = "start" respects strand
mcols(tss) <- mcols(tss)["gene_name"]
tss <- tss[!duplicated(paste(as.character(tss), tss$gene_name))]
length(tss)
tss[tss$gene_name == "APP"]
prom <- tss + 1000                                  # 1000 bp on each side

How many TSSs do you get? Compare with wc -l tss.bed from C2.
Check the APP TSSs against C2b. Why does resize(..., fix = "start") put the TSS of a − strand transcript at its end?
Is tss + 1000 the same set of bases as bedtools slop -b 1000 on the one-base BED TSS? Check the width.



R3 — Fractions at promoters, again
marks <- c("h3k4me3", "h3k27ac", "ctcf")
pk <- lapply(setNames(marks, marks), function(m)
  import(file.path(D, sprintf("gm12878_%s_peaks.bed.gz", m)), format = "narrowPeak"))
sapply(pk, function(p) mean(overlapsAny(p, prom, ignore.strand = TRUE)))
sapply(pk, function(p) length(findOverlaps(p, prom, ignore.strand = TRUE)))

Do the fractions agree exactly with C3? Do the pair counts agree with the default (no -u) line counts?
Why is ignore.strand = TRUE harmless here? (What strand do the peaks have?)



R4 — Distances to the nearest TSS
dist <- lapply(pk, function(p) mcols(distanceToNearest(p, tss, ignore.strand = TRUE))$distance)
sapply(dist, median)
sapply(dist, function(d) mean(d <= 1000))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (m in marks) hist(log10(dist[[m]] + 1), breaks = 60, main = m, xlab = "log10(distance + 1)")

Compare the medians with C5. They differ by a little for some peaks: test with two adjacent ranges, distance(GRanges("chr1", IRanges(1, 5)), GRanges("chr1", IRanges(6, 10))), and the same pair with bedtools closest -d. What is the rule?
Describe the three histograms in one sentence each. Which mark labels promoters, which labels promoters and enhancers, and which is mostly elsewhere?



R5 — Plot the shuffle test
obs  <- 7464                                    # your observed value from C7
shuf <- scan("shuffled.txt"); naive <- scan("shuffled_naive.txt")
hist(shuf, xlim = c(0, obs * 1.05), col = "grey", main = "CTCF peaks overlapping H3K27ac",
     xlab = "overlapping CTCF peaks")
abline(v = obs, col = "red", lwd = 3)
c(restricted = obs / mean(shuf), naive = obs / mean(naive))
What would the histogram look like if the two sets were unrelated?

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — coordinates (B1, B2, R1)





From 1-based [s, e] to BED: start − 1, end unchanged. From BED to 1-based: start + 1, end unchanged. A single base at 1-based position \(p\) is the BED line p−1  p. For the summit: start + peak is a BED boundary; the summit base is start + peak to start + peak + 1 in BED. The narrowPeak format is described on the UCSC format page.









Hint 2 — strand (B3, C2, R2)





On the − strand the gene is read from right to left: the TSS is the largest coordinate, and “2 kb upstream” means 2 kb towards larger coordinates. resize with fix = "start" and promoters use the strand for you.









Hint 3 — bedtools (B4, C3–C7)





Draw it. -u reports each A once if it overlaps anything; -v reports A that overlap nothing; subtract removes the overlapping bases. merge needs sorted input. closest -d reports 0 for overlaps; for non-overlapping intervals bedtools reports one more than the number of bases between them. complement returns the gaps. sort -k7,7gr sorts on column 7 as a general number, largest first.









Hint 4 — shuffling (B7, C7)





Enrichment = observed / mean of the shuffles. Empirical \(p = (k + 1) / (N + 1)\), where \(k\) is the number of shuffles at least as extreme as the observation and \(N\) the number of shuffles. -chrom keeps each interval on its own chromosome; -excl keeps them out of the given regions. See bedtools shuffle and the ENCODE blacklist paper.









Hint 5 — GenomicRanges (R1–R4)





import with format = "narrowPeak" reads the extra columns. overlapsAny, findOverlaps and distanceToNearest are the R versions of intersect -u, intersect and closest -d. gr + 1000 widens a range by 1000 on each side. makeGRangesFromDataFrame has an argument starts.in.df.are.0based.

title: Exercise: Genomic intervals
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) chr7  117559589  117559590. (b) chr2:1001-1250, length 250. (c) chr1  11868  12227, length \(12227 - 11868 = 359\) (in 1-based: \(12227 - 11869 + 1 = 359\)). (d) They touch but do not overlap: the first covers BED boundaries 100–200 (1-based bases 101–200), the second 200–300 (bases 201–300). They share no base, and bedtools intersect reports nothing.
B2. (a) \(53676353 - 53676107 = 246\) bp. (b) Summit boundary \(53676107 + 126 = 53676233\), so the summit base is chr12  53676233  53676234 in BED, position 53 676 234 in 1-based. (c) −1 means not available: the IDR pipeline did not report a \(p\)-value. \(q = 10^{-4.87} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-5}\). (d) No: column 5 is a display score (here 1000 for every strong peak). Rank by signalValue (column 7), or by the \(p\)/\(q\) columns when they are available.
B3. (a) The end, 1 050 000. (b) Upstream is towards larger coordinates: 1-based [1049501, 1052000] (500 bp downstream = 1 049 501 … 1 050 000, 2 kb upstream = 1 050 001 … 1 052 000); BED chr5  1049500  1052000. (c) 998000–1000500: around the annotated start, which for a − strand transcript is its 3’ end. The “promoter” is at the end of the gene, in the last exon or beyond.
B4. (a) chrT 250 300, chrT 850 900. (b) chrT 100 300, chrT 700 900. (c) chrT 500 600. (d) chrT 100 250, chrT 500 600, chrT 700 850. (e) chrT 100 450, chrT 500 600, chrT 700 950. (f) 0 for 100 300 (overlaps B1); for 500 600 the nearest is 250 450, with 50 bases between them (450–499), reported by bedtools as 51; 0 for 700 900. (g) chrT 0 100, chrT 300 500, chrT 600 700, chrT 900 1000.
B5. (a) \(21390 / 53912 = 0.40\). (b) The default reports one line per overlapping pair. A protein-coding gene often has several transcripts with nearby start sites, and each gives its own promoter window; a peak over that promoter overlaps all of them and is reported once per window.
B6. Pairs (1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2). countOverlaps = 1, 2, 1. overlapsAny = TRUE, TRUE, TRUE.
B7. (a) Enrichment \(30 / 12 = 2.5\); \(p = (4 + 1) / (999 + 1) = 0.005\). (b) \(p = (0 + 1)/(99 + 1) = 0.01\); report “\(p \le 0.01\) (none of 99 shuffles reached the observed value)”, together with the enrichment. Run more shuffles if you need a smaller bound. (c) Too high. Shuffled peaks land in places where no real peak can be (centromeres, gaps, unplaced contigs, chrY in a female cell line), so the shuffled overlaps are too low and the ratio observed/shuffled too high.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) H3K4me3 53 912 peaks (mean width 781 bp), H3K27ac 52 455 (1156 bp), CTCF 44 217 (181 bp; median 216, maximum 452). CTCF is a sequence-specific TF: it binds one ~20 bp motif, so its peaks are as narrow as the fragment size allows. Histone marks cover several nucleosomes, and H3K27ac spreads over whole enhancers and promoters. (b) chr1–22 and chrX. No chrY in the CTCF file; one H3K27ac peak on chrY (chrY 15882971 15883161, weak: signalValue 5). C2. (a) -F'\t' splits on tabs only (column 9 contains spaces); $3 == "transcript" keeps transcript lines; the regular expression keeps protein-coding transcripts; match/substr cut the gene name out of the attributes; the TSS is column 4 (start) on + and column 5 (end) on −; GTF is 1-based, so the one-base BED interval is tss − 1, tss. You should get 56 260 lines. (b) The APP gene is chr21 25880535 26171128 −; its TSSs are at 26 140 460 and 26 170 654 … 26 171 128 (BED end column): the large coordinates, the end of the gene. APP has 8 distinct TSSs in GENCODE basic. (c) 56 154 lines. With -k, sort -u compares only the sort keys (chromosome and start), so two TSSs at the same position are collapsed even if they belong to different genes or strands. A silent loss of data.

(b) Promoters of genes that are not protein-coding (lncRNAs, unannotated transcripts); bivalent or weakly active sites, and enhancers, which carry some H3K4me3 when highly active. The weak end of a peak list also contains noise. Including all GENCODE basic transcript start sites raises the fraction from 21 390 to 24 715 peaks (46%).

(H3K4me3’s median is above 1 kb because 60% of its peaks are not at protein-coding promoters, C4.) (b) chr21:5101753-5102097, nearest TSS TPTE at about 5.4 Mb. The CTCF Jaccard is small partly because CTCF peaks are narrow (few bases each), so even complete overlap of every CTCF peak would give a small fraction of the union. Jaccard measures shared bases, not shared sites.

Restricted shuffles: mean about 1120 (range about 1000–1200; the exact numbers depend on the order of lines and the seeds), enrichment about 6.7, empirical \(p = 1/101 \approx 0.01\) (none of the 100 shuffles came close). (b) Naive: mean about 950, enrichment about 7.8: larger, because shuffled peaks fall into regions where no peak can be (B7c). title: Quiz: what is epigenetics?
text:
Short questions on chromatin, histone marks and DNA methylation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Give the narrow (classical) definition of an epigenetic change. Is a histone mark that is put back by transcription factors every time the cell divides “epigenetic” in this sense?






Answer





A mitotically and/or meiotically heritable change in gene function that cannot be explained by a change in DNA sequence (Riggs et al. 1996). A mark that is simply rebuilt by transcription factors after each division is not self-perpetuating, so it is not epigenetic in the narrow sense; the information is carried by the transcription factors. In the broad sense used by “epigenomics” it would still be called epigenetic.




Q2. What is H3K27ac? Where in the genome do you find it, and what does it tell you?






Answer





Histone H3, lysine 27, acetylated. It sits at active promoters and enhancers and marks them as active (as opposed to primed or poised). It is written by p300/CBP and read by bromodomain proteins such as BRD4.




Q3. An MNase digest of chromatin gives bands at about 150, 350 and 550 bp. What are they, and what is the nucleosome repeat length?






Answer





Mono-, di- and tri-nucleosomes: MNase cuts only the linker DNA between nucleosomes. The steps between bands give the repeat length, about 200 bp here (147 bp core + linker).




Q4. A gene has a sharp H3K4me3 peak at its TSS and H3K36me3 over its body. A second gene is covered by a 100 kb domain of H3K27me3. Describe the state of each.






Answer





The first is actively transcribed: H3K4me3 marks its active promoter and H3K36me3 is laid down by SETD2 travelling with the elongating polymerase. The second is silenced by Polycomb (facultative heterochromatin), typical for developmental regulators such as HOX genes in a cell type where they are not needed.




Q5. What is the difference between constitutive and facultative heterochromatin? Give the mark of each.






Answer





Constitutive heterochromatin is compact in every cell type (repeats, pericentromeres, telomeres) and carries H3K9me3, read by HP1. Facultative heterochromatin is silent in some cell types but active in others (developmental genes, the inactive X) and carries H3K27me3, written by Polycomb PRC2.




Q6. Explain how a pattern of CpG methylation is copied when the DNA is replicated.






Hint





What does a CpG look like just after the replication fork has passed?









Answer





CpG is palindromic, so both strands are methylated. After replication each daughter duplex has a methylated old strand and an unmethylated new strand: the CpG is hemimethylated. UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated CpGs and recruits DNMT1, which methylates the new strand. The pattern is copied site by site.




Q7. Why does a histone mark need a “read–write” mechanism to survive many cell divisions, while DNA methylation does not need one in the same way?






Answer





At replication the old, marked histones are split randomly between the two daughters and new unmarked histones fill the gaps, so each daughter inherits only about half of the marks; without re-marking the mark halves at every division (\(0.5^n\)). A writer that is activated by its own mark (PRC2 binding H3K27me3) restores the mark on the new neighbours. DNA methylation is copied from a template at each site by DNMT1, so it is kept directly.




Q8. The human genome has a CpG observed/expected ratio of about 0.25. Why so low, and why are CpG islands an exception?






Answer





Methylated cytosine deaminates spontaneously to thymine, and the resulting T:G mismatch is often repaired the wrong way, so methylated CpGs turn into TpG/CpA over evolutionary time. CpG islands are kept unmethylated (mostly at promoters), so they are not lost and keep a high CpG density (o/e above 0.6).




Q9. In GM12878 B cells the ALB (albumin) gene has no active marks and almost no H3K27me3. HOXD10 has no active marks and a lot of H3K27me3. Both are silent. What is the difference?






Answer





ALB is silent because the activators it needs (liver transcription factors) are absent: nothing opens or marks it. HOXD10 is actively kept silent by Polycomb, a system that represses developmental regulators that must stay firmly off in this cell type. Silence does not always need a repressive mark.




Q10. Genes with high H3K36me3 are highly expressed. Does H3K36me3 activate transcription? How could you test it?






Answer





Not necessarily: H3K36me3 is deposited by SETD2, which travels with the elongating polymerase, so expression causes the mark (reverse causation). Tests: block transcription and see whether the mark disappears; remove the writer (SETD2 knockout) or mutate the residue (H3K36M or K36R) and see whether expression changes.

B1. Counting nucleosomes.

The nucleosome repeat length is 190 bp, of which 147 bp are wrapped around the octamer. How long is the linker?

title: Exercise: What is epigenetics?
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — nucleosome arithmetic (B1, B2)





Linker = repeat − core. Each nucleosome has two copies of each core histone. If the linker is trimmed away, an \(n\)-nucleosome fragment is \(n\) cores plus \(n-1\) linkers; if the cut is in the middle of each linker, it is \(n\) repeat lengths.









Hint 2 — names and marks (B3, B4)





The pattern is histone – residue (one-letter code) – position – modification. K = lysine, S = serine; me = methyl, ac = acetyl, ph = phosphate, ub = ubiquitin. One residue holds one kind of modification at a time; a nucleosome has two copies of H3.









Hint 3 — dilution (B6)





Without re-marking, each division halves the marked fraction: \(0.5^n\). For DNA methylation each site survives one division with probability \(0.999\), so \(0.999^{50}\) after 50.









Hint 4 — CpG o/e (B7, R4)





Count C, G and the dinucleotide CG (read along one strand; overlapping counts like CGCG contain 2 CpGs). Expected CpG = C × G / L. letterFrequency and countPattern do the counting in R.









Hint 5 — reading bigWigs (R1–R3)





import with which = reads only the regions you ask for; as = "RleList" returns one run-length vector per chromosome, which you index by position. promoters and resize respect strand. For ACTB (R2b), compare the gene’s coordinates with the starts of its transcripts.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
About this lecture
Every cell in your body carries (almost) the same genome, yet a neuron and a B cell use very different genes. This lecture is about the layer of information on top of the DNA sequence that helps decide which genes a cell uses, and remembers that decision.

What “epigenetic” means, and why the word is used in two different ways.
Chromatin: how 2 m of DNA is packed into a nucleus, and why packing controls access.
Histone modifications: the marks you will map with ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag.
DNA methylation: the mark you will map with bisulfite and long-read sequencing.
How a state can be remembered through cell division.
A map of the assays in this course, and what each one measures.


This is the first unit of the course and sets up the vocabulary for everything else. Students know transcription and transcription factors from their bachelor’s; most have heard “histone” and “DNA methylation” but few can say what H3K27me3 means or why it should be heritable. The aim today is a working mental model, not a catalogue: by the end they should be able to look at a genome-browser view of a few histone marks and say “this is an active promoter, this is a repressed gene”. Every later unit builds on this.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
One genome, many cell types


A B cell, a neuron and a liver cell share the same DNA sequence, but express different sets of genes.
The identity is stable: a liver cell divides into liver cells, not neurons, long after the signal that made it a liver cell is gone.
So something besides the sequence is (1) different between cell types and (2) copied when a cell divides.


Start from the puzzle that created the field. Cell identity is both different and stable. Transcription factors explain “different”: a liver cell has liver TFs. But TF levels fluctuate and the initial signals during development are transient, so something must also remember. The two candidates we study in this course are chromatin (histones and their modifications) and DNA methylation. Exceptions to “same genome” exist (B and T cells rearrange their receptor genes, somatic mutations), but they do not explain cell identity.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
What does “epigenetic” mean?





Waddington (1940s–50s): the “epigenetic landscape”. A cell rolls downhill into one of several valleys (fates); the genes shape the landscape.
Narrow definition (Riggs et al. 1996): mitotically and/or meiotically heritable changes in gene function that cannot be explained by changes in DNA sequence.
Broad definition (Bird 2007): the structural adaptation of chromosomal regions so as to register, signal or perpetuate altered activity states.



In practice “epigenomics” means measuring chromatin and DNA methylation genome-wide, whether or not the state is heritable.


Two meanings coexist and cause confusion in papers. The narrow, classical one demands heritability: a state that is copied through cell division (mitotic) or even to offspring (meiotic) without a change in sequence. The broad one, which most genomics papers use, calls any chromatin feature “epigenetic”, including states that are rebuilt every time by transcription factors. When a paper says “epigenetic regulation”, ask which one they mean: is there evidence the state is self-perpetuating, or is it just a chromatin mark that correlates with expression? We come back to this in the unit on epigenetic inheritance. Waddington’s landscape is a metaphor, not a mechanism, but it captures the two properties from the previous slide: valleys are different (identity) and walls are high (stability).

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Two meters of DNA in a nucleus
text:
Two meters of DNA in a nucleus


A human diploid genome is 6.4 \times 10^9 bp, about 2 m of DNA, packed into a nucleus about 10 µm across.
Packing is hierarchical: DNA → nucleosomes (“beads on a string”, 11 nm) → loops and domains → chromosome territories.
Packing is not just storage: the more compact a region, the harder it is for proteins to reach the DNA.


Numbers to make it concrete: 0.34 nm per base pair, times 6.4 billion is about 2.2 m. If the nucleus were a football (22 cm), the DNA would be a thread about 40 km long. Each level of the figure is the subject of one part of the course: nucleosomes and their marks (ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq), loops, TADs and compartments (Hi-C). The 30 nm fibre found in textbooks is largely absent in living cells; we skip it. The key message is the last bullet: compaction is a regulatory layer, because a transcription factor or polymerase needs access to its sequence.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
The nucleosome





147 bp of DNA wrapped about 1.7 turns around a histone octamer: two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
Nucleosomes are separated by linker DNA (about 20–80 bp). The linker histone H1 sits where DNA enters and leaves.
Each histone has a flexible tail that sticks out of the particle. The tails carry most of the modifications.



The nucleosome core particle was solved at atomic resolution in 1997 (Luger et al.), one of the key papers. The drawing is simplified to two layers of four histones; in the real structure H3–H4 form a tetramer in the middle, flanked by two H2A–H2B dimers. DNA contacts the octamer every 10 bp or so, where the minor groove faces the histones; this is why some sequences wrap more easily than others. The tails are unstructured and accessible to enzymes, which is why they are the main target of the modifications on the next slides. H1 is not part of the core; it stabilises the more compact forms.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Nucleosomes come in a regular repeat
text:
Nucleosomes come in a regular repeat


Digest chromatin with an enzyme that cuts only linker DNA (micrococcal nuclease, MNase) and you get a ladder: about 150, 350, 550 bp …: one, two, three nucleosomes.
The step of the ladder is the nucleosome repeat length, about 190–200 bp in human cells (147 bp core + linker).
You will see the same ladder in the fragment lengths of every ATAC-seq library.


This is the 1970s experiment that showed chromatin is a repeating unit (Kornberg 1974 proposed the model). The enzyme can only reach linker DNA, so cuts fall between nucleosomes. Fragment sizes are therefore multiples of the repeat length, plus the core. The same logic underlies ATAC-seq: the Tn5 transposase also prefers linker and nucleosome-free DNA, so the fragment-length histogram of an ATAC library has a big nucleosome-free peak under 100 bp, then a mono-nucleosome peak near 200 bp, then di-nucleosomes near 400 bp. Students will compute this in the ATAC units. MNase-seq maps nucleosome positions genome-wide this way.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Nucleosomes block access; regulatory DNA is open
text:
Nucleosomes block access; regulatory DNA is open


Most of the genome is wrapped in nucleosomes. Active promoters and enhancers have a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of a few hundred bp.
Transcription factors bind in the NDR; well-positioned nucleosomes flank it (the +1 nucleosome sits just downstream of the transcription start site, TSS).
“Open” (accessible) chromatin is what ATAC-seq and DNase-seq measure: about 1–3% of the genome in a given cell type.


The NDR is the defining feature of active regulatory DNA. Most transcription factors cannot bind a motif wrapped on a nucleosome; a few “pioneer” factors can (gene-regulation unit), and they open the region for the rest. Chromatin remodelers then slide or evict nucleosomes. The +1 nucleosome is strongly positioned downstream of the TSS; the -1 nucleosome upstream. This figure is the picture students should have in mind when they look at an ATAC-seq peak: a peak is an NDR. The 1–3% number varies with cell type and peak caller, so treat it as an order of magnitude.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Histone tails carry chemical modifications


Enzymes add small groups to amino acids in the tails: acetylation (ac) and methylation (me1, me2, me3) of lysines (K), phosphorylation of serines, and more.
Over 100 different modifications are known. A handful of them are well understood and mapped routinely; those are the ones in this course.
Modifications act in two ways: they change how tightly the histone holds DNA, and they recruit proteins that recognise them.


Point at H3 and H4 tails, which carry the best-studied marks. Lysine acetylation removes the positive charge of the lysine side chain; DNA is negative, so the tail binds DNA less tightly and the chromatin loosens. Methylation does not change the charge: its effect comes almost entirely from proteins that bind methylated lysines. Ubiquitylation of H2A (H2AK119ub, by Polycomb PRC1) and H2B are on the C-terminal tails and are much larger additions. The “histone code” hypothesis (Strahl & Allis 2000) proposed that combinations of marks are read like a code; the modern view is less strict, but combinations do define chromatin states (chromatin-states unit).

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Reading the name of a histone mark
text:
Reading the name of a histone mark


H3K27me3 = histone H3, lysine (K) at position 27, tri-methylated.
H3K27ac is the same lysine, acetylated. One lysine can carry either mark but not both: the two are mutually exclusive, and they mean opposite things.
Positions count from the N-terminus of the mature histone.


A small slide but students need to be able to decode the names fluently, and it is a typical exam question. K is the one-letter code for lysine, S serine, R arginine, T threonine. me1/me2/me3 are mono-, di- and tri-methylation; a lysine can carry up to three methyl groups. H3K27 is a nice example because the same residue is either acetylated (active enhancers and promoters) or tri-methylated (Polycomb repression). Histone variants get their own names: H3.3, H2A.Z, CENP-A (later slide).

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Writers, readers and erasers


Writers add a mark: histone acetyltransferases (HATs, e.g. p300/CBP), lysine methyltransferases (e.g. EZH2, SETD2).
Erasers remove it: histone deacetylases (HDACs), lysine demethylases (e.g. KDM6/UTX).
Readers bind it and bring in other machinery: bromodomains read acetyl-lysine, chromodomains and PHD fingers read methyl-lysine.
Marks are dynamic: they are turned over by writers and erasers, some within minutes.


The writer/reader/eraser framing is the single most useful way to think about any chromatin mark. For each mark you meet in the course, ask: who writes it, who reads it, who erases it. Examples: p300/CBP write H3K27ac at enhancers; BRD4 reads it with its bromodomains and recruits the transcription machinery; HDACs erase it. EZH2 (in the PRC2 complex) writes H3K27me3; KDM6A/UTX and KDM6B/JMJD3 erase it. Many of these enzymes are drug targets (HDAC inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitors, BET inhibitors that block BRD4): see the cancer-epigenetics unit.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Real data: an active gene in B cells
text:
Real data: an active gene in B cells


ENCODE ChIP-seq in GM12878, a B-lymphoblastoid cell line (the course’s main dataset). Each track: enrichment over input (fold change).
H3K4me3 and H3K27ac peak at the promoter; H3K36me3 covers the gene body; H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are absent.


First look at real data, in a genome-browser layout like IGV. Explain how to read a track: x is position along the chromosome, y is how many more reads than in the input control, so a value of 1 means “no enrichment”. The gene model at the bottom shows exons as boxes and the arrow gives the direction of transcription. Point out that the H3K36me3 signal increases towards the 3’ end, as expected for a mark deposited during elongation. The H3K4me1 signal flanks the H3K4me3 peak. The figure is made by make-chromatin-figs.R from ENCODE files listed in data/manifest.tsv; students make the same plots in the exercise.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Real data: two kinds of silence
text:
Real data: two kinds of silence


Left: the HOXD cluster. Developmental genes, silent in B cells, covered by a broad H3K27me3 domain (Polycomb).
Right: a zinc-finger (ZNF) gene cluster on chr19, marked by H3K9me3 (with H3K36me3 over the gene bodies that are still transcribed).
Repressive marks form broad domains (tens to hundreds of kb), not sharp peaks: this matters for peak calling later.


The HOX genes pattern the body axis during development; in a B cell they are off, but they are kept in a repressed state that could in principle be reversed (facultative heterochromatin). H3K27me3 covers the whole cluster, more than 100 kb. The ZNF cluster is the classical place for H3K9me3 in euchromatin; the ZNF genes themselves are transcribed but their 3’ ends carry H3K9me3 together with H3K36me3, an unusual combination. Broad domains matter technically: a peak caller made for sharp TF peaks (MACS default) will cut a broad domain into many fragments, which is why the ChIP units teach broad-domain calling.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Euchromatin and heterochromatin


Euchromatin: open, gene-rich, early-replicating, where most active genes are.
Constitutive heterochromatin: compact, H3K9me3, read by HP1; repeats, pericentromeres, telomeres. The same in all cell types.
Facultative heterochromatin: H3K27me3 (Polycomb); developmental genes silenced in this cell type but active in another.


The terms date from the 1920s (Heitz), when heterochromatin was the part of the chromosome that stayed condensed and darkly stained through interphase. In modern terms it is defined by the marks. HP1 (heterochromatin protein 1) binds H3K9me3 through its chromodomain, dimerises and bridges nucleosomes, compacting the region. In the Hi-C units, heterochromatin is the B compartment, euchromatin the A compartment. In imaging, heterochromatin sits at the nuclear periphery (lamina-associated domains) and around the nucleolus.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Read–write feedback: how a mark can spread and persist
text:
Read–write feedback: how a mark can spread and persist


Some writers carry a reader for their own product. PRC2 (writer of H3K27me3) is activated when its EED subunit binds H3K27me3; SUV39H1 (writer of H3K9me3) has a chromodomain that binds H3K9me3.
A mark therefore recruits more of itself to neighbouring nucleosomes: domains spread until something stops them.
The same loop can restore a mark after it is diluted, which is the key to memory.


This is the mechanism behind both broad domains (previous slides) and inheritance (next slide). Positive feedback makes a state bistable: a region tends to be either fully marked or not marked, and it stays that way. For Polycomb, PRC2 binding to H3K27me3 through EED allosterically stimulates the methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Margueron et al. 2009). Spreading is limited by boundaries such as active transcription, CTCF sites and the turnover by erasers. Mathematical models of this bistability (Dodd et al. 2007) are a good further read for students with a modelling interest.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: Through DNA replication: diluted, then restored
text:
Through DNA replication: diluted, then restored


At replication, old histones (with their marks) are split randomly between the two daughter strands; new, unmarked histones fill the gaps.
Each daughter gets about half the marked nucleosomes. Read–write feedback then re-marks the new neighbours.
Whether histone marks are truly self-sustaining through many divisions is still debated; for H3K27me3 the evidence is strongest.


This is why histone-based memory is harder than DNA methylation: the information is halved at every replication and must be restored from a 50% template. In flies and in mammalian cells, removing the Polycomb recruitment sequence leads to loss of H3K27me3 over a few divisions, which suggests the domain needs both DNA-sequence recruitment and the read-write loop (Laprell et al. 2017; Coleman & Struhl 2017). The plant FLC example later is one of the clearest cases of mitotic memory of a Polycomb state. Be honest with students: this is an active research field, not settled textbook material.

title: What is epigenetics?
section: DNA methylation: a mark on the DNA itself
text:
DNA methylation: a mark on the DNA itself


In mammals, a methyl group is added to carbon 5 of cytosine, almost only in CpG dinucleotides: 5-methylcytosine (5mC).
CpG is palindromic: both strands carry a CpG, and both are usually methylated together.
About 70–80% of CpGs in a human somatic cell are methylated. The exceptions are mostly in CpG islands at promoters.
Plants also methylate CHG and CHH (H = A, C or T).


The methyl group sits in the major groove and does not change base pairing: 5mC still pairs with G, which is why it survives replication as information but is invisible to normal sequencing. Bisulfite sequencing (methylation units) converts unmethylated C to U but leaves 5mC, turning the mark into a sequence difference. Long-read technologies (nanopore, PacBio) detect 5mC directly from the signal. 5mC can be oxidised by TET enzymes to 5hmC, 5fC and 5caC, which are intermediates in active demethylation; bisulfite cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC. In plants the non-CG contexts are maintained by different enzymes (CMT3, DRM2 via RNA-directed DNA methylation), covered in methylation-biology.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Copying DNA methylation through replication


After replication the new strand is unmethylated: each CpG is hemimethylated.
UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated CpGs and recruits DNMT1, which methylates the new strand: the pattern is copied.
DNMT3A/3B methylate de novo (new sites, e.g. during development); TET enzymes start active removal.
Because the template is copied site by site, DNA methylation is the clearest example of a mitotically heritable epigenetic mark.


This is the textbook mechanism for epigenetic memory, proposed in 1975 (Holliday & Pugh; Riggs), and it fits the narrow definition perfectly: the information is in the pattern, and a dedicated enzyme copies it to the daughter strand. Copying is not perfect (about 1 error in 20–1000 CpGs per division depending on context), which is one origin of the drift that epigenetic clocks measure. Passive demethylation happens if DNMT1 is absent or blocked during replication; this is how the primordial germ cells and the early embryo erase most methylation. The de novo enzymes DNMT3A and DNMT3B (Okano et al. 1999) set the patterns in the first place.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
CpG islands


The human genome has only about a quarter of the CpGs expected from its base composition. Methylated C mutates easily to T (spontaneous deamination), so CpGs are slowly lost.
CpG islands (CGIs) are about 1 kb stretches that keep a high CpG density because they are unmethylated. About 60–70% of human gene promoters have one.
CGI promoters are usually unmethylated even when the gene is off; methylation of a CGI promoter means stable silencing (inactive X, imprinted genes, some genes in cancer).


Deamination of C gives U, which repair recognises as foreign; deamination of 5mC gives T, a normal base, so the resulting T:G mismatch is often repaired the wrong way. Over evolutionary time, methylated CpGs become TpG or CpA, which depletes CpG genome-wide (observed/expected ratio about 0.2–0.25). Islands escape because they are protected from methylation, mostly by being bound by transcription machinery and proteins such as CFP1 and KDM2B that recognise unmethylated CpG. The classical definition (Gardiner-Garden & Frommer 1987): at least 200 bp, GC content above 50%, observed/expected CpG above 0.6. In tumours, hypermethylation of CGI promoters silences tumour suppressors (cancer-epigenetics unit).

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Remodelers and histone variants


Chromatin remodelers use ATP to slide, evict or exchange nucleosomes (e.g. SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, INO80 families). They create and maintain NDRs.
Histone variants replace canonical histones at specific places: H2A.Z flanks promoters and enhancers, H3.3 is deposited in active genes independently of replication, CENP-A defines centromeres.


Remodelers are the motors of chromatin: modifications recruit them, and they physically move nucleosomes. SWI/SNF (BAF) subunits are mutated in about 20% of human cancers, which shows how important access is. Variants differ by a few amino acids from the canonical histones but are deposited by dedicated chaperones at specific places. CENP-A is a beautiful example of an epigenetically defined locus: centromeres are defined by CENP-A nucleosomes, not by a specific sequence, and neocentromeres can form on ordinary DNA. H3.3 is also the histone that carries the K27M oncohistone mutation in paediatric gliomas.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Beyond one dimension: the 3D genome


Chromosomes occupy territories; active and inactive chromatin separate into A and B compartments.
Within them, loops and topologically associating domains (TADs) bring enhancers close to the promoters they regulate, often over 10–1000 kb.
Measured with Hi-C (3D genome units).


A teaser only. The point here: a 1D track (previous slides) does not tell us which promoter an enhancer talks to. Loops are made by cohesin extruding DNA until it hits CTCF bound in a convergent orientation; that is why CTCF is in the course dataset. Compartments correlate strongly with the marks: A is H3K27ac/H3K36me3-rich, B is H3K9me3/H3K27me3-rich and lamina-associated. Students will compute compartments themselves from a Hi-C matrix.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Epigenetic memory in action


X inactivation: in female mammals one X is silenced early in development (Xist RNA, H3K27me3, CGI methylation) and stays silent in all descendants.
Genomic imprinting: some genes are expressed only from the maternal or only the paternal copy, set by DNA methylation in the germ line.
Vernalisation in plants: Arabidopsis remembers winter. Cold silences the flowering repressor FLC by Polycomb (H3K27me3), and the silence is kept through cell divisions after it warms up, so the plant flowers in spring.


Three examples that fit the narrow definition: a state set by a transient signal and remembered through mitosis. X inactivation shows memory at the scale of a whole chromosome; calico cats are the visible result of random X inactivation. Imprinting shows memory from the parents’ germ lines: the paternal and maternal copies differ only in methylation at imprinting control regions. The figure uses H19: its imprinting control region is methylated on the paternal allele (set in the male germ line), so H19 is expressed only from the maternal copy. Vernalisation is the plant example (Umeå has a strong plant-science community); it is one of the best-studied cases of quantitative Polycomb memory: the longer the cold, the more cells switch FLC off (an all-or-none switch per cell). The epigenetic-inheritance unit asks which claims of memory across generations hold up.

title: What is epigenetics?
text:
Cause or consequence?


Marks correlate with activity, but correlation does not show that the mark causes it. H3K36me3 is deposited because the gene is transcribed.
Causal tests: replace a histone with a mutant that cannot be modified (e.g. lysine → arginine), tether a writer to a gene (epigenome editing: dCas9 fused to a writer or eraser), or remove the writer.
Treat “epigenetic regulation of gene X” with care: is the mark a driver, a lock that keeps a decision, or a footprint of transcription?


This is the critical-thinking slide and should come back throughout the course. Some marks are clearly downstream of transcription (H3K36me3, H3K79me2). Others act as locks: in flies, replacing all H3 copies with H3K27R derepresses Polycomb target genes, showing the lysine itself is needed for repression. Epigenome editing (dCas9-p300, dCas9-KRAB, dCas9-DNMT3A) can test whether placing a mark changes expression and whether the change is remembered after the tool is gone. Most genome-wide studies, including the ones we analyse, are correlational.

Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Luger et al. 1997, Nature. Crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle at 2.8 Å resolution. The atomic picture of the nucleosome.

Strahl & Allis 2000, Nature. The language of covalent histone modifications. The “histone code” hypothesis.
Barski et al. 2007, Cell. High-resolution profiling of histone methylations in the human genome. One of the first genome-wide maps of histone marks by ChIP-seq.

title: Glossary
text: A running glossary of the biological, technical and analysis terms used in this course. Add terms as the material is written; keep definitions short and link to the unit where the term is taught.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
About this lecture
In RNA-seq you counted reads per gene: the annotation told you where to count. In epigenomics there is no such list. Peaks, domains, CpG islands, loops and methylated regions are all intervals that you find in the data, and most of the analysis is arithmetic on intervals: which overlap, how far apart, how many more than by chance.

Coordinates: genome builds, and the two numbering systems (0-based and 1-based) that cause most off-by-one bugs.
File formats: BED and narrowPeak, GTF, bedGraph and bigWig.
Interval operations with bedtools on the command line.
Is an overlap meaningful? Comparing with shuffled intervals.
The same operations in R with GenomicRanges.


This is a technical unit, but every later unit depends on it. Students are comfortable on the command line and in R, so the new content is the coordinate conventions and the interval logic. The running example uses ENCODE peaks from GM12878 (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, CTCF) and the GENCODE annotation, the same files as in the exercise. By the end they should be able to answer “what fraction of my peaks are at promoters, and is that more than chance?” in a few lines, both with bedtools and in R.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Everything is an interval


A genomic interval is a chromosome, a start, an end and (sometimes) a strand: chr21:33,000,000–33,002,000 (+).
Genes, exons, promoters, peaks, CpG islands, methylated regions, reads, Hi-C loop anchors: all intervals.
Questions about biology become questions about intervals: do my peaks overlap promoters? which gene is nearest? how many reads fall in each peak?


The point of the figure: the same line (a stretch of chromosome) carries many different kinds of intervals, coming from annotation (genes, CpG islands) and from data (reads, peaks). Once everything is an interval, the same handful of operations answers most questions. Counting reads in peaks, which students will do for differential accessibility, is literally the same as counting reads in genes, which they did for RNA-seq; only the intervals differ.

title: Genomic intervals
section: A coordinate only means something with its genome build
text:
A coordinate only means something with its genome build


The reference genome is updated: GRCh37/hg19 (2009) and GRCh38/hg38 (2013) are both still used. The same gene has different coordinates in each.
Chromosome names differ too: UCSC writes chr1, Ensembl/NCBI write 1. Mitochondria: chrM vs MT.
Always check that all your files use the same build and the same naming. Mixing builds gives no error, just wrong answers.
This course uses GRCh38 with chr names throughout.


The most common silent error in interval analysis. bedtools will happily intersect hg19 peaks with hg38 genes and report a few random overlaps. Check the header of the file, the methods section, or test: does a well-known gene’s TSS fall where it should? Converting between builds is done with liftOver (later slide), which is lossy. Also mention the newer telomere-to-telomere T2T-CHM13 assembly, which fills the remaining gaps in GRCh38 and is gaining use, but most epigenomic resources (ENCODE, Roadmap) are still in GRCh38 or hg19.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Two ways to number the bases
text:
Two ways to number the bases


1-based, closed [s, e]: the first base is 1, and the end base is included. Used by GTF/GFF, SAM, VCF, and by genome browsers when they display a position.
0-based, half-open [s, e): count the gaps between bases from 0; the interval runs from gap s to gap e. Used by BED, bedGraph, BAM internally, and most programming languages.
The bases CGT above are chr1:3-5 in 1-based, chr1 2 5 in BED. Length: e - s + 1 in 1-based, e - s in BED.


Draw the ruler on the board. In the 0-based half-open system the numbers label the boundaries between bases, so an interval is “from boundary 2 to boundary 5”, which contains the 3rd, 4th and 5th bases. The advantages: length is end minus start, adjacent intervals share an end/start number, and an empty interval (an insertion point) has start = end. Rule for converting: BED start = 1-based start − 1, end is the same number. The UCSC browser displays 1-based but stores 0-based; that is why a BED line chr1 2 5 shows as chr1:3-5. This slide will be on the exam in some form.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Getting it wrong


Copy a 1-based position from a VCF into a BED file without subtracting 1 and your SNP sits one base to the right: next to the CpG you wanted, not on it.
For peaks of hundreds of bp an off-by-one hardly matters. For single bases (SNPs, CpGs, TSSs, Tn5 insertion sites) it changes the answer.
Tools convert for you when they read a format they know (rtracklayer::import adds 1 to BED starts). Trouble starts when you write files by hand with awk or paste.


A concrete failure, as in the figure: the VCF says the SNP is at 1043 (1-based), the G of a CpG. Written correctly to BED it is chr1 1042 1043; copied as chr1 1043 1044 it sits on the next base, outside the CpG, and an overlap with a CpG list misses it. The same happens to CpG positions from a methylation caller written to BED as pos, pos+1. The fix is boring but important: know which convention each file uses, and convert at the boundary. In the exercise, students make a TSS file with awk from the GTF and have to get exactly this right.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
BED and narrowPeak


BED: tab-separated; three required columns chrom start end (0-based), then optional name score strand and more.
narrowPeak (BED6+4): what peak callers like MACS write. Adds signalValue (enrichment), pValue and qValue (as -\log_{10}), and peak: the summit, as an offset from start.
broadPeak is the same without the summit column, for broad domains.


Walk through the example line (the numbers are illustrative; the exercise starts from real lines of the ENCODE CTCF file). Column 5 (score) is often a scaled integer for display (0–1000) and not a statistic; the statistics are in columns 7–9. pValue and qValue are already −log10, so 10 means 1e-10. Column 10 is easy to misread: it is not a genome coordinate; the summit is start + peak. Summits are useful because the binding site is usually within a few tens of bp of the summit, much narrower than the peak: motif analysis and footprinting use windows around summits. A value of −1 means “not available”: the ENCODE CTCF IDR peaks used in the exercise have pValue −1 in every line.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Annotation: GTF


Gene annotation (GENCODE, Ensembl) comes as GTF/GFF: one line per feature (gene, transcript, exon, CDS, …), 1-based closed.
Column 9 holds attributes: gene_id, gene_name, gene_type, transcript_id, ….
A gene has several transcripts, often with different start sites. “The TSS of a gene” is a choice: the gene start, every transcript start, or a canonical transcript.


Students met GTF files in RNA-seq when counting with featureCounts or building an index, but probably did not look inside. The hierarchy matters: gene lines span all their transcripts; transcripts are made of exons. GENCODE “basic” is a subset with the full-length, well-supported transcripts; we use it to keep files small. The TSS question is a real analysis choice: taking only the gene start can miss alternative promoters, and taking every transcript start counts some promoters many times. In the exercise students use transcript starts of protein-coding transcripts and collapse duplicates.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Strand: where is upstream?


Coordinates always increase left to right along the + strand. A gene on the − strand is read right to left.
TSS = start for a + gene, end for a − gene. Upstream of a − gene means higher coordinates.
“Promoter = 2 kb upstream to 500 bp downstream of the TSS” therefore needs the strand. GenomicRanges::promoters() handles it; bedtools slop -s -l 2000 -r 500 too.


The second classic bug after off-by-one. In the figure, gene A is on + and gene B on −; their promoters point in opposite directions. If you build promoters as start − 2000 to start + 500 for every gene, all minus-strand promoters are in the gene body near the 3’ end instead. In BED, strand is column 6; in GTF column 7. Peaks from ChIP or ATAC have no strand (“.” or “*“), because chromatin has no direction; but the genes they are near do.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Signal tracks: bedGraph and bigWig


A signal track gives a number for every position: reads piled up, divided by a normaliser (CPM, fold change over input).
bedGraph: a BED-like text file, chrom start end value, one line per run of constant value.
bigWig: the same data in a compressed, indexed binary file, with precomputed summaries at several zoom levels. A browser can fetch just the region on screen, even over the internet.


Pileup: count how many reads (or fragments) cover each base. bedGraph compresses runs of equal value into one line. bigWig (Kent et al. 2010) adds an index and zoom levels, which is why a 500 MB bigWig opens instantly in IGV: it reads only the blocks for the current window and the right zoom level. ENCODE provides fold-change and p-value bigWigs for every ChIP experiment; in the chromatin-intro exercise we read regions from them with rtracklayer. Making bigWigs from BAM files is in the reads-to-coverage unit (deepTools bamCoverage).

title: Genomic intervals
section: A genome browser shows intervals and signals together
text:
A genome browser shows intervals and signals together


Real data: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq on chr21. Top: the fold-change bigWig. Middle: the narrowPeak intervals, with summits. Bottom: GENCODE genes.
Peaks are where the signal is high; a summit sits at the top of each peak.
IGV (desktop or igv.js in a browser) loads all of these formats directly.


This is a reconstruction of an IGV view in R (make-intervals-figs.R) so the exact files can be reproduced; in the exercise students load the same files in IGV. Point out a weak signal bump without a peak: the peak caller decided it was not significant. And point out how narrow CTCF peaks are: CTCF is a sequence-specific TF with a long motif, so its peaks are sharp, unlike the broad H3K27me3 domains in chromatin-intro.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
The basic interval operations


intersect: the parts of A that overlap B (or: the A intervals that overlap any B, -u).
subtract / -v: A minus B, or the A intervals that overlap no B.
merge: collapse overlapping (or nearby, -d) intervals into one.
closest: for each A, the nearest B and the distance.
slop / flank: grow intervals, or make windows next to them. complement: the gaps.


Go through each panel with the toy intervals. These six operations, plus coverage counting, cover most of what students will do. Every one exists in bedtools and in GenomicRanges, with slightly different names (table later). Insist on drawing toy intervals by hand when unsure what a command returns: it is faster than debugging.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
What counts as an overlap?


By default, one shared base is an overlap. A 1 bp touch between a 2 kb peak and a promoter counts.
Ask for a minimum: bedtools intersect -f 0.5 (at least 50% of A), -r (reciprocal), or a minimum number of bases (minoverlap in R).
Report choices: one line per pair (default), each A once (-u), or count of B per A (-c). These give different numbers of “overlapping peaks”.


Students are often surprised that “how many peaks overlap promoters” depends on these flags. Default intersect reports one line per overlapping pair, and each line is the overlapping piece, not the whole A interval (use -wa for whole intervals). A peak overlapping two promoters appears twice: if you count lines you overcount peaks. -u fixes that. In the figure the roles of A and B swap between the panels: in the left panel A is the promoters, because -f is a fraction of A. Fraction requirements matter most when comparing peak sets of different widths, for example narrow TF peaks against broad domains. There is no universally right choice; the rule is to state it in the methods.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Sorting and merging


Most tools that walk along the genome need input sorted by chromosome, then start: sort -k1,1 -k2,2n.
bedtools merge collapses overlapping intervals: e.g. peaks from two replicates into one consensus set.
Merging loses the per-interval information unless you ask for it (-c 5 -o max, keep the maximum score).


Sorting: -k1,1 sorts by the first column only (as text), -k2,2n by the second column numerically. Lexical chromosome order (chr1, chr10, chr11, …, chr2) is fine for bedtools, as long as all files use the same order; some tools (bedtools with -g, bigWig tools) want the order of a genome file. Merging peaks from replicates or conditions into a consensus set is the first step of differential accessibility: you need one common set of regions to count reads in.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Nearest feature and distance


bedtools closest -a peaks.bed -b tss.bed -d reports, for each peak, the nearest TSS and the distance (0 if they overlap).
Ties (two TSSs at the same distance) give several lines per peak; -t first keeps one.
The distribution of distances says what kind of element a mark labels: promoter marks sit at 0, enhancer marks kilobases away.


Both files must be sorted. For non-overlapping intervals bedtools reports one more than the number of bases between them (the toy A [900,950) and B [700,800) in the operations figure: 100 bases apart, reported as 101). A signed distance relative to the gene’s direction (-D b) tells upstream from downstream, useful for promoter analyses. Nearest gene is the naive way to assign a peak to a gene; it is right perhaps half the time for enhancers. The integration unit uses Hi-C contacts and activity to do better (ABC model).

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Windows around intervals


slop extends each interval (e.g. ±1 kb around a summit), flank makes windows next to it (e.g. the 2 kb upstream), both strand-aware with -s.
Near a chromosome end, a window would run off the end: these tools need a genome file with chromosome lengths (-g hg38.chrom.sizes) and clip at the end.


Note that flank needs both sides (-l 2000 -r 0); -l alone is an error. The genome file is a two-column text file: chromosome name and length. Download it from UCSC (hg38.chrom.sizes) or make it from a FASTA index (cut -f1,2 genome.fa.fai). The same file is needed for complement, shuffle and genomecov. In R, GRanges carries the chromosome lengths in its seqinfo, and trim() clips out-of-bound ranges.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
bedtools on the command line
# promoter windows: 1 kb either side of each protein-coding TSS
bedtools slop -i tss.bed -g hg38.chrom.sizes -b 1000 > promoters.bed

# H3K4me3 peaks at a promoter (each peak once) vs. not
bedtools intersect -u -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k4me3.bed -b promoters.bed | wc -l

# candidate enhancers: H3K27ac peaks with no H3K4me3 peak and away from TSSs
bedtools intersect -v -a h3k27ac.bed -b h3k4me3.bed \
  | bedtools intersect -v -a - -b promoters.bed > enhancers.bed

# distance from every enhancer to its nearest TSS
sort -k1,1 -k2,2n enhancers.bed | bedtools closest -a - -b tss.bed -d -t first

Every command reads and writes plain text, so they chain with pipes (- means standard input).


These are the exact commands of the exercise, so students see the shape before they type them. The enhancer definition (H3K27ac without H3K4me3, distal from promoters) is a common heuristic and a useful example of building a biological category from interval operations. Point out that wc -l counts lines; with -u each peak appears once, so lines = peaks.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Real data: where do the peaks sit?
text:
Real data: where do the peaks sit?


Distance from each GM12878 peak to the nearest protein-coding TSS.
H3K4me3 peaks pile up at the TSS. H3K27ac is at TSSs and at distal enhancers. CTCF is mostly far from TSSs.


The x axis is log scale (distance + 1). Read the figure as the answer to “what does this mark label?”. The H3K4me3 distribution confirms the promoter mark from chromatin-intro with real data. H3K27ac is bimodal: active promoters and active enhancers. CTCF sites are insulators and loop anchors and are spread through the genome. Numbers on the plot (fraction within 1 kb) are computed in make-intervals-figs.R; students reproduce them in the exercise.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Is an overlap more than chance?
text:
Is an overlap more than chance?


Two sets of intervals will overlap somewhat by chance, more so if they are wide or numerous. A raw overlap count is not evidence.
Null by shuffling: place the same intervals (same widths) at random positions, count overlaps, repeat many times. Compare the observed count with this distribution.
Enrichment = observed / mean of shuffled. Empirical p-value = (number of shuffles with at least the observed overlap + 1) / (number of shuffles + 1).


This is a permutation test, the same idea as in any statistics course, applied to positions on the genome. bedtools shuffle does one shuffle; repeat it in a loop. The p-value can be no smaller than 1/(number of shuffles + 1), so 100 shuffles can at best give about 0.01. For large enrichments, report the fold enrichment and say that none of the N shuffles reached the observed value. Next slide: the real numbers.

title: Genomic intervals
section: Real data: H3K27ac and CTCF overlap more than chance
text:
Real data: H3K27ac and CTCF overlap more than chance


Grey: overlaps between CTCF peaks and shuffled H3K27ac peaks (100 shuffles, same chromosome, same widths). Red: the observed overlap.
The observed overlap is far outside the shuffled distribution: the two sets are associated.


Numbers in the figure come from make-intervals-figs.R. A good discussion point: why do CTCF and H3K27ac co-occur at all, when CTCF is an insulator? Some CTCF sites are at active promoters and enhancers; others are not. The overlap is significant but partial, which a single p-value hides: report the fraction too.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Shuffling has assumptions


A naive shuffle puts intervals in gaps (runs of N), centromeres and unmappable repeats, where real peaks can never be. This inflates enrichment.
Keep shuffled intervals on the same chromosome (-chrom) and inside the mappable, non-blacklisted genome (-incl / -excl).
Peaks also prefer GC-rich, gene-dense regions. The more of that structure the null ignores, the more “significant” everything looks. Choose the background with care; state it.


The general lesson: a p-value is only as good as its null. Here the null is “the intervals could have been anywhere”, and “anywhere” includes places where no assay can produce a peak. Better nulls restrict to the accessible genome, or match on GC content and distance to TSS. Tools such as regioneR (R) and LOLA formalise this; the idea is the same. The same issue comes back with motif enrichment (GC-matched background) and in the ML units (matched negatives).

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Intervals in R: GRanges


GRanges (package GenomicRanges): seqnames, ranges (start, end, width, 1-based closed), strand, and any metadata columns (mcols).
seqinfo holds chromosome names, lengths and genome build: R refuses to compare ranges from different builds if they are set.
rtracklayer::import() reads BED, narrowPeak, GTF and bigWig, and converts BED’s 0-based starts to 1-based.


GRanges is the Bioconductor container for intervals and is used under the hood by DESeq2’s rowRanges, ChIPseeker, DiffBind, csaw, minfi, and many more. Students used SummarizedExperiment through DESeq2; its rowRanges is a GRanges. The seqinfo check is a nice safety net: genome(gr) <- “hg38” on both objects and a comparison with an hg19 object fails loudly instead of silently.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
findOverlaps returns pairs

hits <- findOverlaps(peaks, promoters)      # one row per overlapping pair
queryHits(hits); subjectHits(hits)          # indices into peaks and promoters
peaks[unique(queryHits(hits))]              # each peak once
overlapsAny(peaks, promoters)               # TRUE/FALSE per peak (= bedtools -u)
countOverlaps(peaks, promoters)             # number of promoters per peak (= -c)

findOverlaps is the general operation; everything else is a convenience on top. The Hits object is a two-column table of indices, like a sparse matrix of overlaps. This is the same many-to-many issue as with bedtools default output: one peak can hit several promoters. subsetByOverlaps(peaks, promoters) is the R equivalent of intersect -u.

A reference table; students do not need to memorise it. The key differences: GRanges is 1-based, bedtools 0-based (the numbers in the files differ by one at the start, the bases are the same); reduce() and findOverlaps() respect strand unless you say ignore.strand = TRUE (peaks have strand *, which overlaps both strands, so it rarely bites); distances differ by one: for two ranges that do not overlap, distanceToNearest reports the number of bases between them (0 for directly adjacent ranges), bedtools closest -d reports one more (1 for adjacent). Both report 0 for overlapping ranges. Small differences like these are why comparing the two in the exercise is instructive.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Same bases, different numbers


The BED line chr1  2  5 and the GRanges chr1:3-5 are the same three bases.
rtracklayer::import() and export() convert in both directions. If you read a BED file with read.table() and build a GRanges yourself, add 1 to the start.


The single most common bug when students mix R and the command line: reading a BED with read.table or fread and calling GRanges(chr, IRanges(start, end)) without adding 1. Then every range is 1 bp too long on the left. For peaks it is harmless; for CpGs or SNPs it is wrong. makeGRangesFromDataFrame has a starts.in.df.are.0based argument for exactly this.

title: Genomic intervals
text:
Moving between builds: liftOver


liftOver maps intervals from one build to another using a chain file of aligned blocks (UCSC tool; rtracklayer::liftOver in R).
Some intervals fail (deleted or rearranged in the new build) or split into pieces. Check how many you lose.
Better, when possible: re-align the raw reads to the new build, or download the data already processed in the build you need.


Chain files list blocks of sequence that align between builds and the gaps between them. An interval that spans a gap in the alignment comes out split or not at all. For small intervals (SNPs, CpGs, narrow peaks) liftOver is usually fine; for broad domains and anything near rearranged regions, be careful. ENCODE has reprocessed its data on GRCh38, which is why we use their GRCh38 files directly.

Students should leave able to convert a coordinate between conventions by hand, read a narrowPeak line, build strand-aware promoter windows, answer an overlap question with both bedtools and GRanges, and explain why an overlap count needs a null. Key papers (optional further reading)
